q: Fresh from a few days in a newly coopered cask, a festival sake pours with a distinct resinous scent. Which wood put it there?
exp: Taruzake takes its name from the taru, a cask of Japanese cedar classically cut in Yoshino in Nara, and days rather than weeks is the point, because the fresh wood gives up its resin fast. New Year and shrine celebrations are the style's home ground, where the cask lid is broken open with mallets at kagami biraki.

q: Years in tank turn a sake amber and push its flavour toward soy, caramel and roasted nuts. Which reaction, between residual sugars and amino acids, is doing that?
exp: Koshu carries both reactants in unusual quantity, glucose the ferment left behind and amino acids from the rice, so it browns at cellar temperature with no oxygen involved at all. That is what separates its ambering from the oxidative browning of an old wine, and why even a sealed, topped-up tank of it darkens anyway.

q: Two bottles both read plus three on the sake meter value, yet one tastes markedly drier at the table. What most likely explains the difference?
opts: Higher acidity in the drier one, unseen by the meter
A misprint, since equal readings must taste identical
Added alcohol in the drier one, which the meter reads as sugar
Warmer storage of the sweeter bottle, building extra sugar
exp: The meter is a hydrometer, so residual sugar and density are all it can report, and acid never moves it. Acidity is what turns a given sugar level crisp or cloying on the palate, which is why the trade reads the two figures together and why quoting the meter value alone is guessing.

q: A guest wants the driest sake on the list, and the menu prints every bottle's meter value. Toward which end of the scale should the recommendation move?
exp: Zero is anchored at the density of water: sugar-rich sake is denser and buoys the float higher, putting the waterline at the negative figures, while drier sake lets the float sink and the reading climbs into positive ones. Most premium sake sits between about minus two and plus ten, so a plus sign after the number is the quickest dryness signal a list can carry.

q: Domestic labels print the sake meter value under its Japanese name. Give that name.
exp: Nihonshudo reads literally as Japan sake degree, and export labels translate it as the sake meter value or SMV. Domestic bottles rarely translate it, so recognising the figure beside its plus or minus sign is one of the small literacies a floor sommelier actually uses.

q: Tanrei karakuchi, the light, clean, bone-dry ideal of Niigata brewing, leans on one rice variety that resists dissolving into the mash. Which variety?
opts: Yamada Nishiki
Gohyakumangoku
Koshihikari
Miyama Nishiki
exp: Bred in and for Niigata, Gohyakumangoku has a hard grain that melts reluctantly, so the ferment stays tidy and the sake comes out light and transparent, exactly the local ideal. Yamada Nishiki dissolves generously and builds broader, rounder sake, prized elsewhere and beside the point in tanrei country, while Miyama Nishiki plays a similar workhorse role in cold Nagano.

q: Discovered in Okayama in the mid nineteenth century and never crossbred since, the oldest brewing rice still in commercial use gives deep, earthy, herbal sake. Name it.
exp: About two-thirds of modern brewing rices, Yamada Nishiki among them, carry Omachi somewhere in their pedigree, but Omachi itself is a pure selection from a wayside find, never crossed with anything. It grows tall, ripens late and lodges in wind, and it repays the trouble with a broad, wild, savoury style that has a devoted following.

q: Hired for the season, one figure commands the brewery crew and answers for every tank while the owner keeps to the business side. Give that figure's title.
exp: The toji system was seasonal labour: rice farmers travelled to the breweries after their own harvest, worked the winter under a master trained and placed by a regional guild, Nanbu and Echigo the largest, and went home in spring. Year-round hiring and owner-brewers are eroding the arrangement, but the title stays with whoever commands the brewhouse.

q: Somewhere on the list is a bottle that gentle warming will flatter rather than flatten. Which is the best candidate?
opts: A junmai daiginjo prized for its fragile aroma
A lightly sparkling nigori finished sweet
A yamahai junmai, savoury and high in acidity
A namazake kept chilled since pressing
exp: Warmth magnifies body and umami, and a yamahai's high acidity keeps the warmed sake in balance, which is exactly the yamahai trade; the same degrees strip the esters a daiginjo was fermented cold to keep. A sake that improves with heat is called kan-agari; namazake and anything carbonated are the reliable losers, one for stability and the other for obvious reasons.

q: In the United States a restaurant lists sake by the glass. What is the drink's standing under federal law?
opts: Taxed and labelled as a beer in every respect
Taxed as a beer but labelled under the rules for wine
Treated as a spirit because of its strength
Taxed and labelled as a wine, exactly like a grape wine
exp: The Internal Revenue Code writes sake into its definition of beer, since it is brewed from a grain, so it pays brewery excise; the labelling side runs under the Federal Alcohol Administration Act, which treats sake of seven percent or more like a wine. The split is why sake sits on wine lists and in wine competitions while being taxed like an ale.

q: Japan's Liquor Tax Act refuses the name seishu to any rice brew at or above a certain strength. Where does that ceiling sit?
exp: The same definition demands that the fermenting mash be strained, which is why doburoku, the unstrained farm brew, is legally not sake at all, and why even the murkiest nigori has passed through at least a coarse mesh. The ceiling is also the outer legal wall for undiluted genshu: a rice brew at twenty-two or above changes legal identity, though in practice the yeast gives out first and most genshu land between seventeen and twenty percent.

q: Filled to 50 ml for assessment and holding 215 ml to the brim, which standardised glass does competition tasting specify?
exp: The ISO glass is a controlled variable rather than a fine drinking vessel. Everyone at the bench is then smelling the same volume under the same headspace.

q: A wide, deeply bowled glass is reached for when Pinot Noir is poured. What is that shape doing?
opts: Slowing oxidation once the wine has been poured
Presenting a large surface of wine so aromatics gather
Holding the wine several degrees cooler for longer
Allowing a larger measure without appearing generous
exp: Aromatically subtle, high-acid reds gain from surface area and headspace, and the deep bowl holds what rises off the wine instead of losing it. The narrower Bordeaux shape suits wines whose aromas need no help arriving.

q: Handling a poured glass by the bowl rather than the stem creates which pair of problems?
opts: The glass is weakened at its thinnest point and may break
The wine reads as more tannic and less sweet
Dissolved gas escapes faster from the surface
The wine warms and fingermarks obscure the appearance
exp: Both matter at a tasting bench: a white climbs several degrees in a warm hand, and a smeared bowl makes clarity impossible to judge honestly.

q: A glass leaves the machine carrying a faint chalky bloom. Which two-step remedy is standard before it goes to a table?
accept: hold it over steam then polish
steam then polish with a cloth
ans: Steam and polish with a lint-free cloth
exp: Detergent bloom and water spots survive a machine cycle. Steam softens the film so linen lifts it away instead of smearing it around the bowl.

q: Serious sparkling lists now pour into a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute, chasing which quality the flute suppresses?
exp: A flute shows the bead and hides everything else. Vintage Champagne is a wine before it is a spectacle, and it needs room to be smelled.
